text: Course 6's capstone, the Equipment Checkout scoped application, is now maintained by a small team instead of one developer. The team wants real code review before any change merges — not just an Update Set moving from Dev to Test, but an actual pull request, read and approved by a teammate. This lesson walks that workflow end to end as a worked scenario.

Step one: the team connects the application to a repository, exactly as Lesson 10 described. In Studio, the Equipment Checkout application record is linked to a new GitHub repository, with a service account configured for push and pull access. From this point, the application's code has a real home outside the Dev instance alone.

Step two: a developer is assigned a real piece of work — adding a due-date reminder notification. Instead of editing the main line directly, they create a feature branch for this one change, isolating it from whatever else the team is doing in Dev at the same time. They build the notification in Studio, exactly as Course 6 taught, then push that work so it lands in GitHub as real commits on that branch, not yet merged.

Step three: with the branch pushed, the developer opens a pull request against the application's main branch. A teammate reviews it the way they'd review any other software change — reading the actual diff, leaving a comment on one line of the notification script, and approving only once satisfied. That's the genuine review gate Lesson 9 promised: a visible diff and a conversation, sitting in front of the change before it reaches the shared codebase.

Step four: once approved, the pull request is merged into the application's main branch in the repository — the feature is now officially part of the application's source of truth. The change is then pulled from the repository into the Test instance, updating Equipment Checkout there to match what was just approved, having arrived through a reviewed, documented path rather than an unreviewed Update Set move.

That reviewed, traceable change sitting in Test is exactly what Chapter 4's Automated Test Framework is built to verify automatically, every time it changes again. Source control didn't replace testing — it made the change trustworthy and traceable enough to be worth testing in the first place. Next: what ATF actually tests, starting Chapter 4.
